entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Johannes de Garlandia, a pivotal French music theorist of the late *ars antiqua* period, fundamentally shaped Western musical notation in the late 12th and early 13th centuries. Active primarily within the vibrant intellectual sphere of medieval Paris, his contributions were instrumental in developing precise methods for notating rhythmic modes, a critical advancement beyond earlier, more ambiguous systems. His work provided the foundational grammar for rhythm in polyphonic music, establishing a systematic approach that transcended local practices and laid the groundwork for future musical innovation across Europe.

His treatise, most famously known as *De Mensurabili Musica*, though sometimes titled *De plana musica* and subject to complex authorship debates (possibly representing a school of thought or a compilation rather than a single author), is recognized as the first systematic exploration of measured rhythm in music. Within this seminal text, Garlandia codified the six rhythmic modes, derived from poetic meters, offering a robust framework for organizing musical time. This codification was a watershed moment, enabling the precise transmission and performance of intricate polyphony—a crucial step in the evolution from purely oral and mnemonic musical traditions to a sophisticated written musical language capable of conveying complex rhythmic information. He also contributed significantly to the theoretical understanding of consonances and dissonances.
